title: The Last Mile: From a Survivor to a Pine Script You Can Trust
author: Nhuga_Official
selftext:
https://i.redd.it/wkr2rfqymnvh1.png

You proved the edge is real. This is the unglamorous half — making it reproducible, and the reason a verified backtest still won't match your chart.

15 Oct 2026

# You proved it's real. Now prove you can run it.

Last time I wrote about the overfit gate — the five-stage funnel that separates a durable edge from a well-fit curve, and why the deflated Sharpe is the stage that kills the most "strategies." That post answers one question: is this edge real?

This one answers the question that comes right after — the one almost nobody writes about: can you actually run the thing you just validated, and will it behave the same way on your broker's chart as it did in your research?

Call it the last mile. It's where most quant projects quietly give back the edge they worked so hard to prove.

# A survivor isn't a strategy. It's a signal plus a stack.

When a system clears the gate, what you're holding is a signal — "go long when the 50-EMA is above the 200-EMA," say. But a signal is not a strategy. The thing that actually produces your equity curve is the signal wrapped in an overlay stack: a specific set of decisions that most backtests leave implicit and most screenshots never mention.

There are five overlays that matter, and every one of them changes your results:

* Direction — longs only, shorts only, or both?
* Exit — stop basis, distance, and whether it trails.
* Regime — do you only trade the signal in certain market states?
* Vol-target — do you scale position size to a volatility budget?
* Turnover — do you throttle how often you're allowed to flip?

Leave any of these unspecified and your "strategy" isn't reproducible — it's a mood. The part you forgot to write down is the part that decides your PnL.

# The five overlays, and which ones move your trade list

https://i.redd.it/oohe128xmnvh1.png

Here's the distinction that trips people up: some overlays change which trades you take, and some only change how big each one is. Both move your Sharpe; only the first moves your trade list — and therefore whether your chart can ever line up with someone else's.  


Two details inside the exit overlay deserve names, because they're the usual suspects when two backtests disagree:

* Basis. A close stop checks the bar's close against the level; a touch stop fills at the level the instant price trades through it. Same intention, different fills, different trade list.
* ATR frozen at entry. The stop distance is computed from ATR as it was on the entry bar and then held fixed for the life of the trade. If your code recomputes ATR every bar, you have a different strategy — one that breathes with volatility.

And one trap worth saying out loud: a regime can be tested and not adopted. In several of my gold runs a volatility-regime filter was evaluated, then rejected because it didn't earn its keep out-of-sample. The as-traded system has no regime gate — even though the search looked at one. "Considered" is not "applied."

# The name is not the strategy. The spec is.

Here's what makes this concrete. Across a handful of gold (XAUUSD) runs on different timeframes, the same trend-following family survived more than once. Same idea, same name. But the as-traded systems were not the same strategy:

* On one 4-hour run it survived as a close-basis trailing stop at 5.5×ATR(14).
* On another it survived as a touch-basis fixed stop at 3.5×ATR(14) — fills at the level, distance frozen at entry.
* On a 45-minute run, one export carried no exit overlay at all — a naked signal that simply flips when the moving averages re-cross.

Three survivors from a single idea. Three genuinely different trade lists, different drawdowns, different live behaviour. If I handed you a chart labelled "trend system on gold," you'd have no way to know which of these you were looking at. That's why I now treat the full overlay stack — direction, exit basis, distance, trail/fixed, regime, vol-target, turnover — as part of the system's identity, and stamp it into the script itself.

# Portable means reproducible: Pine that matches the engine bar-for-bar

A strategy that only exists inside your research notebook isn't tradable. So the deliverable is Pine — but Pine that reproduces the research engine exactly, not approximately. Three things make that work:

* One-bar fill. The engine reads a signal on a bar's close and acts on the next bar. In Pine, process\_orders\_on\_close=true reproduces that same one-bar lag, so entries land on the same bars.
* ATR frozen at entry. The stop uses ta.atr(14)\[1\] captured on the entry bar and then held — mirroring the engine's frozen-ATR exit, not a stop that re-reads volatility every bar.
* The direction clamp, injected in order. A long-only system clamps the raw signal with math.max(signal, 0.0) before the exit and sizing logic, in the exact order the engine applies it.

I don't accept "it looks close." I reconstruct the emitted Pine back into the engine's own math and compare bar by bar. On a NIFTY 15-minute series of 80,032 bars, the exit-and-position path came back 0 bars different out of 80,032 — bit-for-bit. That's the bar: if the Pine and the engine disagree on even one bar, the export is wrong. The gold systems in this piece run through that same engine and exporter; the decisive bar-for-bar reconstruction I'm quoting was measured on that NIFTY series — the honest scope of the claim.

(One honest footnote: the deflated-Sharpe number in the header is deflated against the whole search that produced the survivor. Re-run a smaller or larger grid and that number moves — it prices your search, not just your strategy.)

# And yet your TradingView chart still won't match. That's not a bug.

Here's the result that surprises people most. Take that verified Pine, drop it on TradingView over the same dates, and compare it to the research trade list. You find:

* Entries match exactly. Same bars, same entry prices.
* Exits drift. The stop fires a bar early or late, and over a few hundred trades the two lists stop agreeing perfectly.

The instinct is "the code is wrong." It isn't — the code is bit-for-bit, remember. The difference is the data feed.

Your research ran on a specific resampled CSV. TradingView runs on its broker feed. The two don't share the same high and low on every bar — intraday highs and lows especially are feed-dependent. And the trailing stop is driven by ATR(14), which is a running average of true range, which is built from exactly those highs and lows. Different high/low → slightly different ATR → the stop level sits a hair higher or lower → it triggers on a different bar.

Why do entries survive this but exits don't? Because the entry here is a channel breakout or a moving-average crossover — a multi-bar high, or one average crossing another — and those are robust to a little high/low noise. A 14-bar ATR mean is not. The sensitive component is the one that drifts.

(Two more footnotes from the real NIFTY 15-minute comparison: TradingView keeps only \~3 years of intraday history, so you can only honestly compare on the overlap window; and absolute currency PnL will never match, because research runs unit-notional while TV sizes in percent-of-equity — compare return %, not rupees or dollars.)

# What to actually do about it

None of this means the strategy is broken. It means "a backtest" is not a single number — it's a number plus the feed and the spec that produced it. So:

* Pin the feed. Decide which data is ground truth and run both research and live validation on it. If you must use TradingView, seed it with the same bars you researched on — or accept that exits will differ and judge the system on its distribution, not trade-by-trade identity.
* Ship a provenance header. Every script I export carries its full spec in a comment block: the overlay stack, costs, timeframe, and every gate metric (plateau, walk-forward, PBO, DSR). The script is its own documentation — anyone can read exactly what they're running.
* Compare on the overlap window. Don't let a feed that starts in 2023 masquerade as a mismatch against research that starts a decade earlier.
* Compare return %, not currency. Unit-notional research and percent-of-equity execution will never agree on absolute money. They can agree on percentages.
* Treat the overlay stack as the deliverable. "A trend system on gold" is not a handoff. "Long-only trend entry, touch-basis 3.5×ATR(14) stop frozen at entry, no regime, 15% vol-target, on 4-hour bars" is.

# The last mile is where trust is won

The gate tells you whether an edge is real. The last mile — characterize the full stack, verify the export bar-for-bar, document the provenance, and understand exactly why a different feed diverges — is what makes that edge yours to run, not just yours to admire.

A backtest you can't reproduce is a story. A backtest you can reproduce — on a feed you've named, from a script that carries its own proof — is an instrument. Build the instrument.

comments.author: wallneradam
comments.body:
I develop PyneCore, a Pine-compatible Python runtime. One useful check here would be to convert your exported Pine with PyneComp and run it on your exact research CSV, then repeat with TradingView’s exported bars, keeping settings and warm-up history aligned.
That would let you compare your research engine with the exported strategy on identical data, then measure what changes when only the feed changes. It could help establish whether the exit drift comes from the feed or from execution semantics.
Our public TradingView comparison is here: wild.pynesys.io.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The feed point is the useful part here, and you can put a number on it without needing a second data source: nudge the highs and lows by a small random amount, rerun, and count how many exits move by a bar and how much the total return changes. If the result barely shifts, the gap you see on TradingView is just noise. If it shifts a lot, the stop is too tightly tied to one feed's high and low. It's worth publishing that exit-mismatch rate next to the equity curve, since it tells people how much to trust a chart that doesn't line up exactly. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to see how strategy results get compared against a benchmark.
